summary: POC scoping focused on capacity sizing and autoscale for a latency-sensitive assistant workload. Customer wants reserved baseline GPUs for predictability, controlled burst capacity for peak spikes, and clear fallback policies to smaller models or queued responses. Agreed to run a benchmark using customer traffic and define SLOs before the pilot start.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we got about 50 minutes, is this still the right time?
[00:03] Elena Ruiz: Yep, works for us.
[00:06] Jordan Patel: Great. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE, with Maya our Solutions Eng and Liam on the convo too. Quick round robin?
[00:12] Samir Kapoor: Samir here, ML eng, I'll own the POC on our side.
[00:15] Priya Nair: Priya infra, I'll do the network bits.
[00:18] Diego Morales: Diego product, mainly listening for success criteria.
[00:22] Maya Chen: Hi all — Maya. Quick agenda: sizing, autoscale model, benchmarks and timelines, security notes.
[00:28] Jordan Patel: Cool. Elena, can you frame the use case and what success looks like?
[00:32] Elena Ruiz: Sure — Kestrel wants an assistant API embedded into our ops product. Need tail latency under 350ms 95p for short form replies (~80-150 tokens) and about 700ms 95p for longer generations. Cost is a secondary but important metric. We want predictable baseline for business hours and to absorb spikes during launches.
[00:53] Jordan Patel: Got it. So SLOs roughly 95p 350ms for small, 95p 700ms for medium. Any throughput targets? QPS?
[01:00] Samir Kapoor: Typical steady is 20 QPS for small requests, peaks to 120 QPS during heavy runs (release windows). Traffic shape is bursty — lots of short bursts for 2-3 mins.
[01:12] Maya Chen: That maps to two sizing problems — baseline reserved capacity for steady state and a burst or autoscale reserve for the peaks. For POC we usually recommend reserving N GPUs as the baseline and configuring a burst pool that can spin up within X minutes.
[01:25] Priya Nair: What's spin up time look like? We can't have a cold 5 minute lag for user facing.
[01:29] Maya Chen: Good question. With Dedicated reserved GPUs we can keep a warm pool — warm nodes ready to accept traffic with <90s routing time. Cold provision from scratch is longer. We also do prefix caching/KV cache warmup to help common prompts.
[01:42] Jordan Patel: For the POC we can propose a hybrid: reserved baseline GPUs to match 95% daytime load and a hot burst capacity reserved but billed only when used, plus a fallback policy to a smaller model or degraded throughput for extreme spikes.
[01:56] Samir Kapoor: We want to see the economics — if we reserve too much that's wasted. If we reserve too little and depend on cold scale that's a bad UX.
[02:04] Maya Chen: Right. Typical approach: 1) baseline = support steady QPS with headroom (20 QPS steady -> baseline to handle 30-40 QPS), 2) burst pool sized for typical peak delta (reserve some burst GPUs or use capacity tiering), 3) fallback = auto-failover to a 7B model or queue requests with a retry.
[02:20] Diego Morales: How do you decide model fallback vs queue?
[02:23] Maya Chen: Decision rule usually based on latency SLO sensitivity and quality tolerance. If token-quality difference acceptable, route to a cheaper smaller model with similar interface. Otherwise queue and present a progress indicator to user. For the POC we can test both strategies.
[02:37] Jordan Patel: Elena, what's your tolerance for reduced model quality during spikes?
[02:41] Elena Ruiz: Product prefers to keep consistency, but we might accept shorter responses or slightly different phrasing if the semantic is preserved. So fallback to a 7B is okay for non-critical flows, not for billing sensitive transcripts.
[02:55] Samir Kapoor: Ok that helps. For sizing, we can provide a representative 48 hour trace.
[02:59] Jordan Patel: Great. If you share traffic we'll run a benchmark with your prompts and measure p95/p99 and token cost.
[03:06] Maya Chen: On autoscale policy specifics — Redwood supports reactive scaling (util-based), schedule-based (for known peaks), and predictive (traffic pattern learned). For POC we typically combine scheduled scaling for release windows and reactive for unexpected spikes, with a conservative cooldown to avoid oscillation.
[03:23] Priya Nair: Do you support region failover? We need EU data residency for some customers.
[03:28] Maya Chen: Yes — we can pin region and also have fallback region but that crosses data residency boundaries; for EU-only data we'd keep within EU region and instead fallback across instance classes. We'll capture this in the security doc.
[03:40] Jordan Patel: Let's talk numbers — for 20 steady to 120 peak QPS, rough GPU count?
[03:46] Maya Chen: Depends on model. If baseline model is a 13B quantized that can do ~12 tokens/sec per A10032-ish equivalence in our testing for short responses, but these numbers vary. For chat-like 100-token responses, a single GPU might handle ~20-30 short requests per second with batching; so baseline of 2-3 GPUs to give headroom, burst pool of additional 6-8 GPUs to hit the 120 QPS peak. If you use a 70B model, the counts are lower and you'd need more GPUs.
[04:15] Samir Kapoor: We're leaning 13B for cost/quality. Good to see numbers. Can you run benchmarks for 13B vs 70B?
[04:22] Maya Chen: Yes, benchmark plan: run your 48hr trace through our testing harness with both models and quantization profiles, measure p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec cost, KV cache hit rate. We'll also test warm vs cold starts and a burst warm pool.
[04:35] Jordan Patel: Timeline — if we get logs by Friday (2026-06-12), we can schedule the benchmark next week (week of 6/15) and share results mid-week. POC kickoff would be after benchmark agreement — maybe start 6/22 if all green.
[04:49] Elena Ruiz: That timeline works. We'll aim to deliver the logs by Friday.
[04:53] Diego Morales: On SLOs, can you expose per-route SLOs and dashboards?
[04:56] Maya Chen: Yes Redwood Console will show per-route latency and cost, and we can set alerts for SLO breaches. We'll include tracing hooks so you can tie a failing prompt to model version.
[05:06] Samir Kapoor: About pricing — curious about reserved vs on-demand mix. If we reserve baseline GPUs what commitment are we looking at for the POC?
[05:13] Jordan Patel: For POC we usually do a short-term reserved pool (monthly commit) that gives lower unit rates and optional burst pool billed at a higher rate only when used. We'll send a couple options: minimal baseline commit and a medium commit to reduce burst consumption.
[05:25] Priya Nair: Network and security — we need VPC peering, SAML SSO, and KMS integration. Also audit logs retention.
[05:33] Maya Chen: All supported. For Private deployments we can do VPC-only control plane. For Hosted Dedicated we'll set up VPC peering and KMS integration. Audit logs available with configurable retention. We'll attach the security checklist.
[05:45] Elena Ruiz: Any limits on concurrent KV cache sessions? We use per-customer KV caches to speed up repeated prompts.
[05:51] Maya Chen: KV cache is per-model session and scaled with the pool; memory limits depend on instance size. We'll capture recommended memory/profile counts in the benchmark report — and show cache warmup improvements.
[06:02] Jordan Patel: Let's cover fallback policies concretely for POC: 1) auto-fallback to 13B quantized from 70B when p95 > SLO, 2) queue with progress token if model unavailable >30s, 3) degrade to shorter responses. Any objections?
[06:18] Samir Kapoor: Ok on 1 and 3. For billing transcripts we want to avoid quality hits; maybe exclude those routes from fallback.
[06:25] Maya Chen: That's typical — per-route policies. We'll configure exclusion lists.
[06:30] Diego Morales: What's the rollback behavior if a rollout impacts latency?
[06:33] Maya Chen: Redwood supports automated rollout and automatic rollback on regression tied to your eval sets/prompts. We can enable canary traffic and auto-failover to previous version.
[06:42] Priya Nair: Are there quotas we need to be aware of for burst billing?
[06:46] Jordan Patel: We'll include soft limits with alerting; you can cap burst spend.
[06:50] Samir Kapoor: Benchmark details — please include p99 measurements.
[06:53] Maya Chen: Will do. We'll run synthetic and replay of your real traffic.
[06:57] Jordan Patel: Any legal/procurement constraints?
[06:59] Elena Ruiz: We'll need SOC2 Type II and standard DPA. Procurement will review pricing but this POC is low friction.
[07:06] Jordan Patel: Ok wrapping: action items and delivery dates as we discussed. We'll send pricing and the autoscale/fallback doc, you send logs. Schedule benchmark for the week of 6/15.
[07:16] Diego Morales: Sounds good. Thanks.
[07:18] Jordan Patel: Thanks everyone.
[07:20] [meeting end]
